title: How does bus policy square with Scotland's looming budget black hole?
excerpt: THE old saying goes, “when you are in a hole, stop digging”. It is generally accepted that the Scottish Government are heading towards a financial hole in the next couple of years. Its exact size is yet to be determined but it may well be in the region of £5 billion.
content:
THE old saying goes, “when you are in a hole, stop digging”. It is generally accepted that the Scottish Government are heading towards a financial hole in the next couple of years. Its exact size is yet to be determined but it may well be in the region of £5 billion.

Cabinet Secretary for Public Service Reform Ivan McKee (pictured) has been tasked with attempting to fill the hole while at the same time trying to avoid compulsory redundancies. Good luck with that, Ivan.

At last week’s SNP conference the First Minister announced his intention to, in effect, nationalise the nation’s bus infrastructure.

READ MORE: SNP to bring Scotland's buses into public control, John Swinney says

I am sure we would all be interested to learn the operational and financial arrangements behind this policy. Presumably the current owners and shareholders would be entitled to some degree of financial compensation.

A war of words has already commenced. Sandy Easdale, who owns McGill’s with his brother James, said “Swinney appears to have transformed into the next Idi Amin or Robert Mugabe. Both men bankrupted their countries through catastrophic financial policies.”

Ralph Roberts, chairman of McGill’s, accused the First Minister of trying to confiscate their business and claimed the SNP’s plans could cost the taxpayers hundreds of millions of pounds each year.

READ MORE: McGill's threatens legal action as SNP defend public control plans

No doubt the Easdale brothers will already be consulting their lawyers. Expensive court cases look very possible, with the Scottish taxpayer, as usual, being asked to finance the Scottish Government case.

If, in the end, the Scottish Government is successful, presumably the compensation price of the bus infrastructure will simply add to its already considerable financial problems and the hole will simply get bigger.

As yet there appears to be no financial information available as to the net cost of “reforming” both local government and the health service.

Bringing buses under public control, local government and health service reform may well be laudable ideas – but at any cost? Each and every day more than 14,000 Scottish children remain in temporary accommodation. The eventual cost of bus nationalisation could build a whole lot of affordable new homes.

Anne Laird
Inverness

JANE McLeod’s piece, “Trade unionist blasts trans rights ‘censorship’” (Oct 17), reports that Mike Corbett, an official at Scottish teaching union NASUWT, has condemned the BBC for obscuring “Protect the Dolls” from a T-shirt worn on Strictly Come Dancing. Mr Corbett insists that the slogan is not political but an “absolute necessity” and accuses the BBC of censorship.

But “Protect the Dolls” is not simply an appeal for kindness or safety. It is a campaigning slogan associated with trans-rights activism, communicating solidarity with a particular political movement and its objectives.

READ MORE: 25 MSPs commit to Scottish conversion practices ban

A cause does not cease to be political merely because its supporters regard it as morally self-evident. Political movements routinely present their objectives as matters of justice, safety or necessity. Calling a political demand an “absolute necessity” does not make it non-political or place it beyond legitimate debate.

Indeed, Corbett’s decision to wear the slogan while addressing an SNP conference fringe event rather underlines its political character.

Mr Corbett is entitled to express his political opinions, but neither he nor anyone else is entitled to have the BBC broadcast them, particularly on an entertainment programme.

The BBC says removing slogans and overt branding is standard editorial practice. Applying that practice to a campaigning slogan is not evidence of censorship, it is called impartiality.

There is considerable irony in Mike Small’s article, “The erasure of normal people” (Oct 18), in which he condemns the erasure of dissenting voices while engaging in that very practice himself.

READ MORE: Mike Small: The pathetic censorship of late-stage Britain cannot be hidden

Small glibly states that “‘Dolls’ is how the LGBT+ community refers to trans women.” On what authority does he presume to speak for lesbians, gay men and bisexual people as though we all use that term, let alone share a common position on “gender identity”?

Being attracted to members of one’s own sex does not entail believing that sex can be changed, that gender identity supersedes biological reality, or that particular political slogans speak for us. No-one would make such assumptions about heterosexual people. By invoking an imaginary consensus within an “LGBT+ community”, Small effectively renders dissenting LGB voices invisible.

For a writer so concerned about the erasure of people whose views depart from approved orthodoxy, his apparent inability to recognise the very same phenomenon when he perpetrates it is remarkable.

Brian Forsyth
Edinburgh

UNLIKE my MP, Dave Doogan, I do not object to Andy Burnham, and others, describing Manchester as being in the “North of the UK”. Paradoxically, taking umbrage at this error implies that one wishes Scotland to be, correctly, identified as the north of the UK, a political state of affairs an increasing majority of Scots actually resent and wish to end. Let Mr Burnham, and a probable majority of the English, plough on irritating us by their Anglo-centric ignorance, I say.

David Roche
Blairgowrie

Trip to Dunfermline was interesting, but tinged with sadness

IN a previous letter I referred to Scotland as “a proud nation since 832AD”, when the Picts defeated the Northumbrians at the Battle of Athelstaneford and our national flag, the Saltire, was born. A more traditionally accepted statement would have referred to Scotland as “a proud nation since 843AD”, when the Picts and the Scots were allied under King Kenneth MacAlpin. From this period through to the Union of the Crowns in 1603 and the Acts of Union of 1707, apart from the exploits of Wallace and Bruce, Scotland’s history remains a mystery to most Scots while most Scots are familiar with events pertaining to the reins of King Harold II (Bayeux Tapestry – arrow in the eye), Richard I (“Lionheart”) and Henry VIII (plus his many wives) of England.

An overdue visit to Dunfermline Abbey and the nearby museum at the weekend proved enjoyably interesting but tinged with sadness. While conservation efforts at the Abbey of the Kings and the adjacent palace are to be lauded, as well as the helpful efforts of the informative staff, the empty structures of the “Auld Kirk” and the palace bear witness to a massive hole in Scotland’s proud history.

READ MORE: Archaeologists find remains of 200-year-old fortified wall in Glasgow

The Reformation of 1560 robbed Scotland of much of its remaining visible historical legacy, including the “Royal Tombs” (documented by E Henderson) of kings and queens (including Saint Margaret, 1045-93), princes and princesses, which were smashed and destroyed, leaving the identities of bodies buried underneath unidentified (apart from the accidentally rediscovered lead-shrouded skeleton of King Robert The Bruce).

It seems ironic that at the home of the world-famous philanthropist, Andrew Carnegie, these tombs have not been recreated or reimagined to a level that would encourage visitors not only from other parts of Scotland and the rest of the UK , but from around the world, to visit this historic site.

The hollow shell of the Auld Kirk structure, supported by the zig-zag columns which are evidence of Norman influence in its construction (12th-century Romanesque architecture) could be turned into a magnificent hall housing marble statues and tombs representing Scotland’s early kings and queens along with presentations of their individual stories.

The brass plate representation of King Robert The Bruce over his coffin is impressive (although effectively hidden behind the modern pulpit), but in spite of his name prominently carved out in the top of the abbey tower, and a cast of his skull presented nearby the pulpit, there is no imposing statue of the inspirational man who famously led the Scots to victory over the English at Bannockburn in 1314.

A plan has already been proposed to maintain the buildings and transform this site into a nationally significant cultural heritage and pilgrimage destination, which hopefully can be realised with public financial support. A truly imaginative transformation could ensure this site not only has historic international significance but is a compelling must-visit world heritage destination.

Stan Grodynski
Longniddry, East Lothian

I AM a retired Scot living in southern Spain. I was born in Scotland and spent all my working life there. As a British citizen with residency in Spain,

it is my right to remain in the electoral register and I have used my vote as often as I can. Unfortunately I am only allowed to vote in General Elections. I was really disappointed to discover that the Scottish Parliament elections are considered local elections and I wasn’t allowed to vote.

As a Scot I think of this as my national parliament, not a local election. My concern is that if there is a referendum on Scottish independence, would I have a vote? Other countries, like France, have MPs for their overseas citizens. I would like to see Scotland do the same.

Carolin Rebecca
